title: Barn Façade County
summary:
Carl Ginet's case, published by Alvin Goldman in 1976: Henry is driving in the country and, looking at an object in a field, says to himself, "That's a barn." It is a barn, and he sees it perfectly well. But, unknown to Henry, the district is full of barn façades: fronts with nothing behind them, which look exactly like barns from the road. He happened to look at the only real one.

Did Henry know it was a barn? Most people say no, although nothing went wrong in his own seeing: he was right, but he could as easily have been fooled. Goldman used the case to argue that knowing means being able to tell the real thing from the look-alikes around it; later writers say knowledge must be "safe", true in all the nearby ways things could have gone.
citations: Alvin I. Goldman, "Discrimination and Perceptual Knowledge," Journal of Philosophy 73(20) (1976): 771–791 (the case is credited to Carl Ginet)
Edmund L. Gettier, "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?", Analysis 23(6) (1963): 121–123
Jonathan Jenkins Ichikawa and Matthias Steup, "The Analysis of Knowledge," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/knowledge-analysis/
